newsitem.title: UK: Rothschild to prove independent banks can survive.
newsitem.headline: Rothschild to prove independent banks can survive.

text.p: With nearly 200 years of history behind it, the Rothschild banking dynasty has no intention of seeing its independence slip away as the millennium approaches.

For Sir Evelyn de Rothschild, chairman of the merchant banking group's parent company, has a mission to prove there is a place for banks such as his in the rapidly changing world of global investment banking.

"In my working time in the City I've seen about 12 merchant banks disappear. I want to prove independent merchant banks like Rothschilds, Schroders and Flemings have a huge role to play in the international financial scene," Rothschild told Reuters on Tuesday.

Speaking as the merchant banking group broke with tradition and published its annual results -- which showed a 66 percent rise in operating profits for the group worldwide -- Rothschild trumpeted the cause of Britain's independent investment banks.
"We are one of the key players as an independent. There's too much talk about the fact that we are dodoes about to disappear down the plughole, and we are still here," he added.
The foundations for today's Rothschilds group were laid nearly 200 years ago when the five sons of Mayer Amschel Rothschild began setting up banks in the main cities of Europe.

N M Rothschild & Sons, the main operating company in Britain, has been based at New Court in the City of London for nearly 200 years. The firm celebrates its 200th anniversary next year, Rothschild said.
Speculation about the group's future has been intense since the suicide a year ago of a leading member of the family, Amschel Rothschild, who was chairman of Rothschild Asset Management.

This not only led to questions about who would succeed Sir Evelyn, who is 65 and has been at the firm for 40 years, but also suggestions the group could be swept up by one of the larger investment banks trying to carve a bigger slice of the world market.
With firms such as SG Warburg, Kleinwort Benson, Barings and Smith New Court all now part of other larger organisations, the number of independent investment banks has dwindled.
But while Rothschild, which confirmed it had established a global partnership to improve its service to customers, may not have the muscle of the big banks, it believes it can compete with them.
To Rothschild this requires being extremely quick.
"One of the strengths as an independent organisation like Rothschilds is we can make decisions quickly," he said.
He also believes there is a conflict for larger banks, which not only lend to clients but also advise them. And he is not convinced they can survive in the "one-stop" format they have developed.

"To be all things to all people is not necessarily the answer to the banking fraternity. The customer is what really matters, the customer wants to feel that the relationship is full of integrity and is responsible and the advice given is independent and totally constructed for his benefit," Rothschild said.
Rothschild's approach has the backing of its shareholders, the family whose name it bears.
Rothschild said they are keen to keep it under family ownership, while recognising the organisation is a meritocracy where non-family members can get into top positions within the business.
"There may one day be a non-Rothschild chairman, a non-Rothschild chief executive," he added.
And while the family tradition can be a useful tool for the benefit of the group as a whole, it must not be solely for the family's benefit.
Rothschild sees the solid support offered by the family ownership as one of the main reasons why people are happy to work at the firm.

He points out that other banks have disintegrated or been swallowed up by larger rivals because of fractured shareholdings, where shareholders have not been interested in continuity and problems have developed as a result.
In Rothschild's case, the family has not on the whole been "rapacious" and has acted in the best interests of the business, Rothschild said.
"Next year we celebrate 200 years of N M Rothschild here in London and I like to think we may go on for another 200 years," he said.
Asked how much longer he would be at the helm of the historic firm, Rothschild was unambiguous.
"I'm here as long as they want me to stay, I haven't any other interests," he said.
But his involvement in the day-to-day running of the business has diminished, with his role now concentrated on management matters and selling the Rothschild name and its expertise.
"I'm a salesman for the business, a flag-waver if you like," Rothschild said.
